deck.title: Elastic Load Balancing & Auto Scaling
deck.analogy: A load balancer is the restaurant host at one front door: guests know one address, the host seats them at free tables and skips broken ones, while the Auto Scaling manager adds or removes tables to match how busy it is.

subtopics.title: OSI layers in 60 seconds (you need this to pick the right LB)

cards.front: What three things does an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) provide for a fleet of EC2 instances?

back.answer: One DNS name, traffic spread across many servers, and health checks that stop sending traffic to sick servers.
back.explanation: When a sick server recovers, the ELB sends traffic to it again.
back.mnemonic: The restaurant host: one front door, seats guests at free tables, skips broken tables.

cards.front: In the classic AWS architecture, what role does an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) play behind the Elastic Load Balancer?

back.answer: Adds or removes EC2 instances to match demand and replaces failed instances, growing and shrinking behind the ELB.
back.explanation: ELB out front, ASG behind it — the classic self-healing architecture.
back.mnemonic: The restaurant manager who adds or removes tables as it gets busy.

cards.front: In the OSI model, what does a Layer 3 (Network) load balancer see?

back.answer: Only IP addresses — which building the traffic goes to.
back.mnemonic: Layer 3 = the address on the envelope.

cards.sourceHeading: OSI layers in 60 seconds (you need this to pick the right LB)

cards.front: What does a Layer 4 (Transport) load balancer see beyond Layer 3?

back.answer: The IP address plus the port (e.g., TCP 443 or UDP 3000) — the building and the door inside it.
back.mnemonic: Layer 4 = the envelope address plus the apartment number (the port).

cards.sourceHeading: OSI layers in 60 seconds (you need this to pick the right LB)

cards.front: What can a Layer 7 (Application) load balancer inspect that lower layers cannot?

back.answer: HTTP details: the URL path, headers, cookies, and hostnames.
back.mnemonic: Layer 7 = the mail carrier opens the envelope and reads the letter.

cards.sourceHeading: OSI layers in 60 seconds (you need this to pick the right LB)

cards.front: How does the OSI layer an ELB works at determine the routing decisions it can make?

back.answer: Layer = how deep it looks into traffic. L4 balancers can't route on URL paths but are very fast; L7 balancers route on content.
back.explanation: That trade-off is the whole ALB-vs-NLB story.

cards.sourceHeading: OSI layers in 60 seconds (you need this to pick the right LB)

cards.front: At which OSI layer does an Application Load Balancer (ALB) operate, and which protocols does it support?

back.answer: Layer 7; HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC.
back.explanation: Its superpower is smart routing by path, host, or header.

cards.front: At which OSI layer does a Network Load Balancer (NLB) operate, which protocols does it support, and what is its superpower?

back.answer: Layer 4; TCP, UDP, and TLS. Superpowers: extreme speed plus a static IP.

cards.front: At which OSI layer does a Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) operate, and what is its job?

back.answer: Layer 3 (IP packets, GENEVE). It sends traffic through fleets of third-party security appliances.

cards.front: How should you treat the Classic Load Balancer (CLB) on the SAA-C03 exam?

back.answer: As legacy with no modern superpower — if CLB is an answer option, it is wrong.

cards.front: Which three kinds of content-based routing can an Application Load Balancer (ALB) perform?

back.answer: Path routing (/api/*), host routing (app.example.com vs admin.example.com), and header/query-string routing.
back.explanation: Only a Layer 7 balancer reads HTTP, so only an ALB can route on content.

cards.front: Which target types can an Application Load Balancer (ALB) route to?

back.answer: EC2 instances, private IPs, Lambda functions, and containers (ECS) — grouped into target groups.

cards.front: An app behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) needs the original client IP — where does it find it?

back.answer: In the X-Forwarded-For header — the ALB terminates the client connection, so targets otherwise see the ALB's IP.
back.explanation: The ALB opens a new connection to the target.

cards.front: Which load balancer can AWS WAF attach to, and why?

back.answer: Only the ALB — WAF inspects HTTP, which requires Layer 7, so it cannot attach to an NLB.

cards.front: What do sticky sessions do on an Application Load Balancer (ALB), and when are they the answer?

back.answer: A cookie pins a user to the same target — the quick fix for legacy apps that store session state locally.
back.explanation: Better design: externalize session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB.

cards.front: How does dynamic port mapping let an Application Load Balancer (ALB) pack ECS containers densely?

back.answer: Multiple containers of the same app run on one instance on random ports, and the ALB tracks and routes to each.

cards.front: Customers must whitelist a fixed IP for your Application Load Balancer (ALB) — what is the trap?

back.answer: An ALB gives a DNS name, not a static IP, so it cannot do this. Put an NLB in front or use Global Accelerator.
back.explanation: Whitelisting fixed IPs needs NLB static/Elastic IPs or Global Accelerator.

cards.front: What performance profile makes the Network Load Balancer (NLB) the "extreme performance" exam answer?

back.answer: Millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency.

cards.front: Why is a Network Load Balancer (NLB) the choice for gaming, IoT, MQTT, or custom binary protocols?

back.answer: It speaks any TCP or UDP traffic. An ALB only handles HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC and cannot do UDP.

cards.front: What IP addressing does a Network Load Balancer (NLB) offer that an ALB does not?

back.answer: One static IP per AZ, and you can assign your own Elastic IPs — the whitelisting answer.

cards.front: How does a Network Load Balancer (NLB) handle the client source IP by default?

back.answer: It preserves the client source IP — targets see the real client with no header tricks needed.
back.explanation: Contrast the ALB, which requires reading X-Forwarded-For.

cards.front: Which load balancer is required in front of a PrivateLink endpoint service?

back.answer: An NLB (or an ALB behind an NLB) sits in front when you expose your app privately to other VPCs.

cards.front: What is the one job of a Gateway Load Balancer (GLB)?

back.answer: Transparently push all traffic through a fleet of third-party security appliances (IDS/IPS, next-gen firewalls, deep packet inspectors) before it reaches your app.
back.explanation: "Inspect traffic with third-party / partner security appliances" → GLB, every time.
back.mnemonic: A bump in the wire: in one side, through the appliances, out the other — nobody changes IP addresses.

cards.front: Which protocol and port does a Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) use?

back.answer: The GENEVE protocol on port 6081.

cards.front: What problem does cross-zone load balancing solve on an Elastic Load Balancer?

back.answer: Without it, each LB node sends traffic only to targets in its own AZ; cross-zone spreads evenly across all targets in all AZs.
back.explanation: If AZ-a has 2 instances and AZ-b has 8, the AZ-a pair gets hammered without cross-zone.

cards.front: Compare the cross-zone load balancing defaults and costs for ALB vs NLB.

back.answer: ALB: on by default and free. NLB: off by default, with inter-AZ data charges when enabled.

cards.front: What does connection draining (deregistration delay) do on an ELB, and what is its default?

back.answer: On target removal or scale-in, the LB stops new requests but lets in-flight requests finish gracefully; default 300 seconds.
back.explanation: "Users get errors during scale-in" → tune deregistration delay.

cards.front: How does SNI (Server Name Indication) let one load balancer host multiple TLS certificates?

back.answer: The client says which hostname it wants during the TLS handshake, and the LB serves the matching certificate.
back.explanation: "Host many HTTPS domains on one ALB" → SNI.

cards.front: What is TLS termination on an Elastic Load Balancer?

back.answer: The LB decrypts HTTPS itself (certificate usually from ACM) and can talk plain HTTP to targets, offloading crypto work from instances.
back.explanation: TLS = Transport Layer Security, the encryption behind the "s" in https.

cards.front: What does a launch template define for an Auto Scaling Group (ASG), and what is the legacy alternative?

back.answer: The instance recipe: AMI, instance type, security group, user data, key. Launch configurations are the legacy version — prefer templates.

cards.front: How do min, desired, and max work in an Auto Scaling Group (ASG)?

back.answer: The ASG always steers actual count toward desired, clamped between min and max; scaling policies work by changing desired.

cards.front: What happens in an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) when an EC2 instance dies?

back.answer: The ASG replaces it automatically — self-healing capacity for free.

cards.front: What does a Target Tracking scaling policy do in an ASG, and what is its exam keyword?

back.answer: "Keep this metric at this value" (e.g., CPU at 40%) — AWS does the math. Keyword: simplest, "maintain X%".

cards.front: What does a Step Scaling policy do in an ASG?

back.answer: Adds or removes N instances at metric thresholds you define — fine-grained thresholds.

cards.front: When is Scheduled scaling the right ASG policy?

back.answer: When load is predictable at known times — "every Monday 9am", month-end batch.

cards.front: What does Predictive scaling do in an ASG?

back.answer: Machine learning forecasts load from recurring patterns and scales ahead of it — "proactively".

cards.front: What is the default ASG warm-up/cooldown period, and what problem does it prevent?

back.answer: 300 seconds. It stops the ASG from counting a booting instance as still overloaded and over-scaling in bursts.
back.explanation: "ASG launches too many instances in bursts" → cooldown/warm-up.

cards.front: THE trap: the load balancer marks instances unhealthy but the ASG never replaces them — why, and what is the fix?

back.answer: Default ASG health checks are EC2 status checks only. Enable ELB health checks so the ASG replaces app-dead instances.
back.explanation: An instance can run fine while its app is crashed or returning 500s; only the LB sees that.

cards.front: In the ASG + SQS worker pattern, what metric should drive scaling?

back.answer: A custom metric of backlog per instance — ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by instance count — with target tracking, not CPU.
back.explanation: "Scale workers based on pending jobs" → SQS queue depth drives the ASG.

cards.front: What is the default ASG termination policy during scale-in (who dies first)?

back.answer: Balance AZs (most instances first), then oldest launch template/configuration, then closest to the next billing hour.

cards.front: Compare Route 53 failover vs ELB failover vs ASG replacement: which disaster does each survive?

back.answer: Route 53 survives a region dying (DNS, minutes, TTL-bound); ELB survives an instance dying (in-path, near-instant); ASG replaces the dead instance.
back.explanation: ELB is fast, in-path, within a region; Route 53 failover is DNS-based, slower, across regions. Serious architectures use both.

cards.front: You must route /api/* to one set of servers and /images/* to another. Which load balancer do you choose?

back.answer: Application Load Balancer with path-based routing — only Layer 7 sees URLs.

choices.why: Layer 4; blind to URL paths.
Only L7 reads URLs, enabling path-based routing.
Pushes traffic through security appliances, not HTTP paths.
Legacy; always the wrong answer.

cards.front: A UDP-based multiplayer game needs low latency and a static IP. Which load balancer fits?

back.answer: Network Load Balancer — an ALB cannot do UDP or static IPs.

choices.why: No UDP support and no static IP.
For third-party security appliance fleets.
L4 speed, UDP support, static IP per AZ.
Legacy; always the wrong answer.

cards.front: You must inspect all traffic with a third-party firewall/IDS appliance fleet. What do you deploy?

back.answer: Gateway Load Balancer — GENEVE 6081, bump-in-the-wire through the appliance fleet.

choices.why: Transparently sends traffic through third-party appliance fleets (GENEVE 6081).
Routes HTTP content; not an appliance bump-in-the-wire.
Fast L4 forwarding, not appliance inspection.
WAF needs Layer 7; cannot attach to an NLB.

cards.front: The load balancer marks instances unhealthy, but the Auto Scaling Group never replaces them. What fixes this?

back.answer: Enable ELB health checks on the ASG — the default is EC2 status checks only.

choices.why: Cooldown delays scaling actions; it doesn't change the health source.

choices.text: Enable ELB health checks on the ASG
choices.why: ASG then trusts the LB's app-level verdict and replaces dead instances.
Balances traffic across AZs; unrelated to health replacement.

choices.text: Switch to a newer launch template
choices.why: Changes the instance recipe, not health detection.

cards.front: Payroll traffic spikes every month-end at a known time. Which ASG scaling policy fits?

back.answer: Scheduled scaling — predictable timing means scale on a schedule.

choices.why: Reacts to metrics, not known times.
ML forecasting is overkill for known times.
Reacts at metric thresholds, not clock times.
Known, predictable times = scheduled actions.

cards.front: You must keep average CPU at 40% with minimal configuration. Which ASG scaling policy?

back.answer: Target tracking — "keep metric at value" plus "simplest".

choices.why: "Keep this metric at this value"; AWS does the math, simplest option.
Needs you to define thresholds and step adjustments manually.
For known times, not maintaining a metric value.
No automation; won't maintain the metric.

cards.front: One ALB must serve many HTTPS domains, each with a different certificate. Which feature enables this?

back.answer: SNI (Server Name Indication) — multiple TLS certificates on one listener.

choices.why: Pins users to targets via cookie; unrelated to certificates.
Client names the hostname in the TLS handshake; LB serves the matching cert.
Spreads traffic across AZs; unrelated to certificates.
Lets in-flight requests finish during removal; unrelated to certificates.

cards.front: Corporate clients must whitelist fixed IP addresses for your load balancer. What do you use?

back.answer: Network Load Balancer with Elastic IPs (or Global Accelerator in front of an ALB).

choices.why: An ALB provides a DNS name, never a static IP.
Legacy; always the wrong answer.
For security appliance fleets, not client whitelisting.
Static IP per AZ; you can assign your own Elastic IPs.

cards.front: An app behind an ALB needs the original client IP. How does it get it?

back.answer: Read the X-Forwarded-For header. (An NLB would preserve the source IP natively.)

choices.why: ALB terminates the connection and passes the real client IP in this header.
Pins users to targets; doesn't reveal the client IP.
Balances across AZs; doesn't reveal the client IP.
Moves decryption, but targets still see the ALB's IP.

cards.front: Workers in an ASG must scale based on the number of unprocessed jobs. What should drive the ASG?

back.answer: SQS queue depth — ideally backlog per instance (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible ÷ instance count), not CPU.

choices.why: Idle workers can show low CPU while the queue fills.
For known times, not a changing job backlog.

choices.text: SQS queue depth (backlog per instance) metric
choices.why: Queue depth tracks pending work; target tracking on backlog per instance.
Network traffic doesn't measure unprocessed jobs.

cards.front: You must handle millions of TCP requests per second with extreme performance. Which load balancer?

back.answer: Network Load Balancer — "millions" plus "ultra-low latency" means Layer 4.

choices.why: L7 HTTP smarts cost speed; not the extreme-performance answer.
For security appliance fleets, not raw performance.
Legacy; always the wrong answer.
Millions of requests per second at ultra-low latency.

cards.front: Keyword: **"Path / host / header routing"**

back.answer: ALB

cards.front: Keyword: **"HTTP, microservices, containers, Lambda target"**

back.answer: ALB

cards.front: Keyword: **"WAF on a load balancer"**

back.answer: ALB (L7 only)

cards.front: Keyword: **"UDP, extreme performance, millions req/s"**

back.answer: NLB

cards.front: Keyword: **"Static IP / Elastic IP / whitelisting"**

back.answer: NLB (or Global Accelerator)

cards.front: Keyword: **"PrivateLink endpoint service front"**

back.answer: NLB

cards.front: Keyword: **"Third-party security appliances, GENEVE 6081"**

back.answer: GLB

cards.front: Keyword: **"Classic Load Balancer"**

back.answer: Wrong answer

cards.front: Keyword: **"Multiple TLS certs, one LB"**

back.answer: SNI

cards.front: Keyword: **"Errors during scale-in"**

back.answer: Deregistration delay (draining)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Uneven traffic across AZs"**

back.answer: Cross-zone LB (ALB free/on, NLB paid/off)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Client IP behind ALB"**

back.answer: X-Forwarded-For

cards.front: Keyword: **"\"Keep CPU at X%\" simply"**

back.answer: Target Tracking

cards.front: Keyword: **"Known time spikes"**

back.answer: Scheduled scaling

cards.front: Keyword: **"ML-forecasted scaling"**

back.answer: Predictive scaling

cards.front: Keyword: **"ASG ignores app-level failures"**

back.answer: Enable ELB health checks on ASG

cards.front: Keyword: **"Scale on job backlog"**

back.answer: SQS queue depth metric

cards.front: Keyword: **"Instance-level failover"**

back.answer: ELB (in-path, instant)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Region-level failover"**

back.answer: Route 53 (DNS, slower)
